assessment.name: Year 8 Computing Autumn assessment
assessment.sections: In your first Computer Science lesson in the week of 30 November, on Chromebook (45 minutes).
assessment.weighting: Revision booklet lessons 1 to 10: digital fluency (files, footprint, privacy, ethics, law), computer systems (CPU, RAM, storage, fetch decode execute, input and output) and networks (LAN, WAN, internet and the web).

mock.note: 30 questions across all ten lessons in the revision booklet.

units.name: Digital footprint, personal data and privacy
Inside a computer and the fetch decode execute cycle
Networks, the internet and the web

cards.title: Files, folders and cloud storage
cards.question: How should you organise and store your files?
points: A file is a digital object that stores data. A folder organises files; a subfolder is a folder inside another folder.
A file extension shows the file type, such as .docx (Word document) or .jpg (picture).
Local storage saves files on your own device and works without the internet.
Cloud storage saves files on online servers, such as OneDrive (Microsoft's cloud storage). Synchronisation keeps files up to date across devices.
cards.watch_out: Cloud storage needs an internet connection. A disadvantage is that you cannot reach your files offline, and you rely on the provider's security.
cards.hook: Local = on your laptop. Cloud = on the internet.
cards.grade9: Suggest a clear filename that describes the work, such as Y8_Networks_Revision, so it is easy to find later.

cards.title: Digital footprint and online identity
cards.question: What is a digital footprint, and what is the difference between active and passive footprints?
points: A digital footprint is the trail of information and data you leave when using the internet.
Active footprint: information you deliberately share, such as posts, comments and photos.
Passive footprint: data collected about you without you directly sharing it, such as a website recording your visit.
Your online identity is how you present yourself and are represented online. Metadata is data about data, such as the time, date or location of a post.
cards.watch_out: Deleted posts may still exist, because others could have saved or screenshotted them.
cards.hook: Active = you Act. Passive = it happens while you Pass by.
cards.grade9: Explain how an unkind comment could harm your own online identity in the future, such as when applying for a job.

cards.title: Personal data and privacy
cards.question: What is personal data, and how can you keep it private?
points: Personal data is information that identifies or can be linked to a person, such as a name or address.
Sensitive data needs extra protection, such as health information.
Privacy means keeping personal information safe and controlling who can access it.
Consent means freely giving permission for information to be collected or used. Privacy settings control who can see your information and contact you.
cards.watch_out: Never share your password or home address publicly, even with friends online.
cards.hook: THINK before sharing, CHECK the settings, PROTECT your accounts.
cards.grade9: Before allowing an app to use your location, check why it needs it, who will see it and whether you can turn it off.

cards.title: Staying safe with apps and accounts
cards.question: What should you check before giving information to an app or website?
points: Only give information when it is necessary and the request is trustworthy.
Check privacy settings on apps, games and social media.
Use strong passwords and keep them private.
Ask a trusted adult if an app requests information you are unsure about.
cards.watch_out: Free apps often collect data to make money, so read what they ask for.
cards.grade9: Explain the link between privacy and safety: less personal data online means fewer chances for strangers to find or impersonate you.

cards.title: Ethics and law
cards.question: What is the difference between ethics and law?
points: Ethics are ideas and principles about what people believe is right or wrong.
A law is a rule made by an authority that people must follow.
An action can be possible online, and even legal, but still be unkind, unfair or unethical.
Ask permission before sharing another person's photo or information, and respect their privacy, work and choices.
cards.watch_out: Ethical means right or wrong; legal means following the law. They are different questions.
cards.grade9: If a friend leaves their account open, the ethical choice is to log them out or tell them, not to read or post anything.

cards.title: The Computer Misuse Act
cards.question: What does the Computer Misuse Act do?
points: It is a UK law that makes unauthorised access to computer systems and certain forms of misuse illegal.
Unauthorised access means accessing a computer, account or data without permission.
Example: a student guesses a teacher's password and opens their files. This is unauthorised access and is illegal.
Cybercrime is illegal activity involving computers, devices or networks.
cards.watch_out: Even just looking at files without permission counts. You do not have to change anything to break the law.
cards.grade9: Explain why changing someone's data without permission is both an ethical and a legal issue.

cards.title: The Data Protection Act
cards.question: What does the Data Protection Act do, and what are the main principles?
points: It is a UK law that controls how personal data is used and protected.
The data subject is the person whose personal data is being processed.
Organisations should collect only the data they need, use it for a clear purpose and keep it accurate.
Data should be stored securely and not kept longer than necessary, then deleted.
cards.watch_out: The Data Protection Act is about personal data held by organisations. Hacking into accounts is covered by the Computer Misuse Act.
cards.hook: DPA protects Data; CMA stops Misuse.
cards.grade9: Explain why old data should be deleted: the less data kept, the less can be stolen in a data breach.

cards.title: CPU, RAM, storage and motherboard
cards.question: What do the main parts inside a computer do?
points: CPU (Central Processing Unit): processes instructions and controls the computer.
RAM (Random Access Memory): temporary memory holding programs and data currently in use. It is volatile.
Secondary storage (SSD or HDD): saves files, programs and the operating system long term. It is non-volatile.
Motherboard: the main circuit board that connects the components so they can communicate.
cards.watch_out: Volatile memory loses its contents when the power is switched off. RAM is volatile; storage is not.
cards.hook: CPU thinks, RAM remembers for now, storage remembers for ever.
cards.grade9: Explain opening a program: it is loaded from storage into RAM, then the CPU fetches and runs its instructions from RAM.

cards.title: The fetch decode execute cycle
cards.question: How does the CPU process instructions?
points: Fetch: the CPU retrieves the next instruction from RAM.
Decode: the CPU works out what the instruction means.
Execute: the CPU carries out the instruction.
The cycle repeats continuously for each instruction while programs run.

example.heading: Adding two numbers
lines: Fetch the add instruction from RAM
Decode it: the CPU works out it must add two numbers
Execute it: the CPU adds the numbers and stores the result

cards.watch_out: The order is always Fetch, Decode, Execute. After fetching, the next stage is decode.
cards.hook: Get it, understand it, do it: Fetch, Decode, Execute.
cards.grade9: Explain why it is called a cycle: after executing one instruction, the CPU immediately fetches the next.

cards.title: Input, process and output
cards.question: What are input, processing and output?
points: Input is data entered into a computer. Input devices: keyboard, mouse, microphone, touchscreen, webcam.
Processing is working on data using instructions.
Output is the information produced. Output devices: monitor, speakers, printer, headphones.
Data is raw facts and figures; information is processed data that has meaning.
cards.watch_out: A touchscreen is both an input and an output device.
cards.grade9: Explain the difference between data and information with an example: 18, 21, 19 is data; the average temperature this week was 19 °C is information.

cards.title: Networks: LAN and WAN
cards.question: What is a network, and what is the difference between a LAN and a WAN?
points: A network is a group of connected devices that communicate with each other.
LAN (Local Area Network): covers a small area, such as a school or home.
WAN (Wide Area Network): covers a large area, such as a country or the whole world.
Wireless means connecting without cables. Networks allow resource sharing: sharing files, printers and internet access.
cards.watch_out: The internet is the biggest example of a WAN.
cards.hook: LAN = Little Area. WAN = Wide (Whole world) Area.
cards.grade9: Give an advantage and a disadvantage of networks: sharing resources, but viruses can spread between devices.

cards.title: The internet and the World Wide Web
cards.question: What is the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web?
points: The internet is a worldwide network of connected networks: the infrastructure.
The World Wide Web (WWW) is a service that uses the internet: all the websites and webpages.
A website is a collection of webpages. A webpage is an individual page on a website.
A browser is software used to access websites, such as Chrome. Other internet services include email and video calls.
cards.watch_out: The internet and the web are not the same. Email uses the internet but is not part of the web.
cards.hook: Internet = the roads. Web = the shops along the roads.
cards.grade9: Use the road analogy to explain why other services, like online games, also travel on the internet.

cards.title: Keyword check
cards.question: Can you define each of these keywords?
points: Synchronisation, active footprint, passive footprint, metadata.
Personal data, sensitive data, consent, privacy settings.
Ethics, Computer Misuse Act, Data Protection Act, unauthorised access, data subject.
CPU, RAM, volatile, secondary storage, fetch, decode, execute.
LAN, WAN, internet, World Wide Web, browser.
cards.watch_out: Cover the definitions in the booklet and test yourself on each word.
cards.hook: Say it, define it, give an example.

written.q: Explain how the CPU, RAM and storage work together when you open a program.
model: The program is stored long term in secondary storage, such as an SSD (1)
When opened, it is loaded into RAM (1)
The CPU fetches each instruction from RAM, decodes it and executes it (1)
RAM is used because it is much faster for the CPU to access than storage (1)

written.q: A student guesses a teacher's password and reads their files. Explain why this is both unethical and illegal.
model: It is unethical because it invades the teacher's privacy (1)
They did not give consent for anyone to see their files (1)
It is illegal because it is unauthorised access (1)
This breaks the Computer Misuse Act (1)

written.q: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
model: The internet is a worldwide network of connected networks (1)
The World Wide Web is a service that uses the internet (1)
It is made of websites and webpages viewed in a browser (1)

exam_tips.timing: 45 minutes on the Chromebook. About a minute per question; check your answers at the end.
section_a: Learn the keyword tables in the revision booklet word for word.
Watch out for pairs that are easy to mix up, such as active and passive, LAN and WAN, internet and web.
Read all the options before choosing.
section_b: Use the keywords in full sentence answers.
Give an example with every definition.

section_b.For law questions, name the law: Computer Misuse Act or Data Protection Act.

grade9: Describe what each part does and what happens next: keyboard, CPU, display.
Trace one program in order: stored on the SSD, loaded into RAM, then fetched, decoded and executed by the CPU.
